emergency.note: 119 covers both fire and ambulance; English interpretation is available, and #7119 gives non-emergency medical advice.

avoid.reason: Very safe; in Kabukichō (Shinjuku) avoid touts and "free drink" bars — inflated-bill scams

hood_desc: A dense, neon-lit hub of skyscrapers, department stores, izakayas and the sprawling Kabukicho nightlife district. Suits travelers who want nonstop energy, dining and entertainment around the clock.
The iconic youth-culture and fashion center famous for its scramble crossing, trend-setting shops and vibrant nightlife. Ideal for those chasing street style, pop culture and lively crowds.
Tokyo's most elegant and upscale district, lined with flagship luxury boutiques, fine dining and refined art galleries. Best for visitors seeking sophisticated shopping and polished dining.
An atmospheric old-town area centered on the ancient Senso-ji temple, rickshaws and traditional craft shops. Perfect for travelers wanting a taste of historic, nostalgic Tokyo.
The world-renowned electronics and otaku district crammed with anime, manga, gaming and gadget shops plus quirky maid cafes. A haven for tech lovers and pop-culture fans.

water.note: Tap water is treated to a very high standard and safe to drink.

transit.pay: Get a Suica or Pasmo IC card — it works on virtually every train, subway and bus. Buy one at station ticket machines (¥500 deposit, ~US$3.50), pick up a deposit-free Welcome Suica for tourists at the airports and major JR stations, or add Suica to an iPhone or Android in seconds. Top up with cash at any station machine or convenience store.
transit.hours: Trains and subways run about 5am to midnight–1am; there are no night trains, so plan for a taxi after the last train.

landmarks: Tokyo Skytree
The world's tallest tower (634m), offering sweeping observation-deck views over the entire Tokyo metropolis.
Sensō-ji Temple
Tokyo's oldest and most iconic Buddhist temple in Asakusa, known for its giant Kaminarimon lantern gate.
Shibuya Crossing
The world's busiest pedestrian scramble crossing, an electrifying symbol of Tokyo's urban energy.
Meiji Shrine
A serene Shinto shrine set within a forested park, dedicated to Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken.
Tokyo Tower
A red-and-white Eiffel Tower-inspired landmark that has symbolized Tokyo's postwar rebirth since 1958.
Shinjuku Gyoen National Garden
A beautifully landscaped garden blending Japanese, French, and English styles, especially famous for cherry blossoms.
Tokyo Imperial Palace
The primary residence of Japan's Emperor, set behind moats and stone walls in the heart of the city.
Takeshita Street, Harajuku
A vibrant, narrow shopping street packed with youth fashion, crepe stands, and eye-popping street style.
teamLab Planets TOKYO
An immersive digital art museum in Toyosu where visitors wade through water and light-filled installations.
Ginza
Tokyo's premier upscale shopping and entertainment district, dazzling with neon signage and flagship stores.

train.note: Japan is an island network with no international trains. Book Shinkansen heading north and east on JR East's Eki-Net; for the Tokaido Shinkansen to Nagoya, Kyoto and Osaka use JR Central's smartEX (smart-ex.jp/en). Most Shinkansen leave from Tokyo Station.

bus.note: There are no international buses from Japan. For cheap long-distance and overnight travel, Willer Express (willerexpress.com/en) and the JR Bus group (kousokubus.net/JpnBus/en) run big highway-bus networks from the Busta Shinjuku terminal and Tokyo Station.

ferry.note: Tokyo has no international passenger ferries - boats to South Korea sail from western ports like Fukuoka, Shimonoseki and Osaka, far from Tokyo. From Tokyo's Takeshiba pier, Ogasawara Kaiun (ogasawarakaiun.co.jp/english) runs the 24-hour domestic voyage to the remote Ogasawara Islands, and Tokai Kisen (https://www.tokaikisen.co.jp/english/) sails overnight and by jet boat to the Izu Islands.
